summary: This Standards Track document defines three hybrid key agreement mechanisms for TLS 1.3: X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768, and SecP384r1MLKEM1024. They combine post-quantum ML-KEM with an elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman exchange.

eli5.summary: Two locks work together on a door, one old and one new, so the door stays shut unless both are broken.

subtitle: Three TLS 1.3 key agreement groups that pair post-quantum ML-KEM with a classic elliptic curve exchange.

tldr.problem: ML-KEM is designed to withstand quantum computers, but it is newer than elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman. TLS 1.3 needs a way to use both together so a connection stays secure as long as one of them holds.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC applies the hybrid framework of RFC 9954 to ML-KEM and defines three supported groups: X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024. Each concatenates the ECDHE and ML-KEM key shares and shared secrets.
tldr.outcome: IANA registered code points for all three groups, and only X25519MLKEM768 is marked Recommended. The same registration obsoletes two earlier pre-standard Kyber768 draft entries.

today: RFC 10024 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2026. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it obsoletes the two Kyber768 draft entries in the IANA registry.

sections.title: Why Hybrid Key Agreement
sections.content:
ML-KEM is a key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) defined in NIST FIPS 203. It is designed to withstand cryptanalytic attacks from quantum computers.

RFC 9954 defines a framework for combining a traditional key exchange with a next-generation one in TLS 1.3. The goal is security against both classical and quantum adversaries while staying compatible with existing infrastructure. This RFC applies that framework to ML-KEM and specifies the code points for the resulting hybrid groups.

In the RFC's terms, ECDHE with Curve25519, P-256 or P-384 is traditional, and ML-KEM is next-generation. A hybrid exchange uses several algorithms at once and combines their outputs, so security holds as long as at least one component stays secure.
sections.eli5: Two different kinds of lock guard the same door. Putting both on means a thief needs to break both.

sections.title: The Three Groups
sections.content:
The RFC introduces three new TLS 1.3 supported groups, each combining ML-KEM with an ephemeral elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE) exchange as described in RFC 9954.

  • X25519MLKEM768 uses X25519 (RFC 7748). The RFC calls it widely deployed and often the most practical choice for a single hybrid combiner in TLS 1.3.
  • SecP256r1MLKEM768 uses secp256r1 (NIST P-256). It supports use cases that require both shared secrets to come from FIPS-approved mechanisms.
  • SecP384r1MLKEM1024 uses secp384r1 (NIST P-384). It is meant for high-security environments that need FIPS-approved mechanisms with an increased security margin.

Any of the three may be implemented in a FIPS-approved way.
sections.eli5: There are three versions of the double lock: a popular everyday one, one for places that follow government rules, and a stronger one for places that need extra safety.

sections.title: Key Shares and Shared Secrets
sections.content:
In TLS 1.3, the client sends a key_exchange value and the server answers with its own. For these groups each value is a concatenation of an ECDHE part and an ML-KEM part. The client's ML-KEM part is an encapsulation key. The server's ML-KEM part is a ciphertext produced by encapsulating to that key.

The order differs by group. For X25519MLKEM768 the ML-KEM part comes first in both shares and in the shared secret. The RFC notes that this reverses the naming convention of RFC 9954 for historical reasons. For the two NIST curve groups the ECDHE part comes first. The ECDHE share is the uncompressed point encoding from RFC 9846.

Sizes in bytes are fixed per group (see the table below). The resulting shared secret is the concatenation of the ML-KEM and ECDHE shared secrets.
sections.eli5: Each side sends a package with two pieces inside, one for each lock. The final secret is also made of two pieces glued together.

sections.title: Required Checks
sections.content:
Implementations MUST validate what they receive and abort the handshake on failure.

  • The server MUST run the encapsulation key check from Section 7.2 of NIST FIPS 203 on the client's encapsulation key, and abort with an illegal_parameter alert if it fails.
  • The client MUST check that the ciphertext length matches the selected group, and abort with illegal_parameter if not. If ML-KEM decapsulation fails for any other reason, the connection MUST be aborted with an internal_error alert.
  • Both sides MUST process the ECDHE part as in RFC 9846, with all validity checks, and abort with illegal_parameter on failure. That includes the all-zero shared secret check for X25519.
sections.eli5: Before using the package, each side checks that it is the right size and shape. If anything looks wrong, they stop right away.

sections.title: Regulatory Context
sections.content:
This informal section relates the groups to NIST guidance. All three permit FIPS-approved key derivation under NIST SP 800-56C and SP 800-135. SP 800-56Cr2 approves HKDF (RFC 5869) with two distinct shared secrets, provided the first is computed by a FIPS-approved key-establishment scheme.

FIPS also needs a certified implementation, which the RFC says will stay more common for secp256r1 in the coming years. That explains the ordering: ML-KEM first in X25519MLKEM768, ECDHE first in the other two. So for the NIST curve groups the ECDHE implementation must be certified and ML-KEM need not be, while for X25519MLKEM768 the ML-KEM implementation must be certified.

The RFC also says the groups follow the principles of NIST SP 800-227, Section 4.6, on combining post-quantum and classical key establishment.
sections.eli5: Some places have rules about which locks must be officially approved. The order of the pieces is chosen so the approved lock goes first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 9954 apply. The analysis relies on the TLS 1.3 message transcript, so one cannot assume a similar hybridization is secure in other protocols. All three groups use fixed-length public keys, ciphertexts and shared secrets, as RFC 9954 requires. Implementers are encouraged to use implementations resistant to side-channel attacks, especially remote ones.

Randomness gets special attention. The ML-KEM encapsulation randomness is encrypted and then recovered by the client, so anything it reveals about the random generator's other outputs is exposed to the client. An insecure generator whose output is disclosed can be attacked, as shown in the Dual EC work the RFC cites. Implementers should follow the guidance in NIST FIPS 203 and Appendix C.1 of RFC 9846, and may use mechanisms from RFC 8937. If one insecure generator feeds both algorithms, a disclosure by one also affects the other.
sections.eli5: The locks need good random numbers for their keys. If the random numbers are guessable, a clever thief could work out more than they should, so use a really good dice roller.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered three entries in the TLS Supported Groups registry. They are for use with the final NIST version of ML-KEM in FIPS 203.

All three are marked DTLS-OK. Only X25519MLKEM768 is marked Recommended.

The RFC also obsoletes two experimental entries for pre-standard Kyber768, X25519Kyber768Draft00 (25497) and SecP256r1Kyber768Draft00 (25498). IANA changed their Recommended field to D and pointed their comment at this RFC.
sections.eli5: Each group gets its own official number in a big public list, and the old test versions are marked as retired.
